title: Characteristics of object-oriented languages
summary: Objects as data plus behavior, encapsulation through privacy with the AveragedCollection example, why Rust has no inheritance, and the two things inheritance is used for: code reuse and polymorphism.

sections: TRPL 18.1 Objects Contain Data and Behavior
TRPL 18.1 Encapsulation That Hides Implementation Details
TRPL 18.1 Inheritance as a Type System and as Code Sharing

blocks.md: There is no single agreed definition of **object-oriented programming** (OOP). The features usually named are objects, encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism. Rust supports some directly, some differently, and one not at all. Knowing which is which helps when you bring habits from Java, C# or Python.

blocks.title: OOP features in Rust

privacy: fields and functions are private unless `pub`

blocks.title: Encapsulation
blocks.md: Encapsulation means the details of how an object works are hidden from code using it; the only way to interact is its public API. *The Rust Programming Language* shows a collection that keeps a cached average. Its fields are private, so outside code cannot change the list without updating the average:

blocks.explain: Because `list` is private, the implementation could later switch to a `HashSet` or keep a running sum instead of re-adding, and no caller would need to change. That freedom is the point of encapsulation.

blocks.title: No inheritance, and what to use instead
blocks.md:
Inheritance lets a type take on another type's data and behavior without redefining them. Rust has no way to define a struct that inherits a parent struct's fields and methods. It is a deliberate choice: inheritance often shares more than intended, couples subclasses tightly to their parents, and in many languages allows only one parent anyway.

Programmers reach for inheritance for two reasons, and Rust has an answer for each:

1. **Code reuse.** Write a method once, use it for many types. In Rust: **default methods** in a trait (chapter 10), which implementors get for free and may override. For data, use **composition**: put the shared struct inside the others as a field.
2. **Polymorphism.** Use a child type wherever the parent is expected. In Rust: **generics** with trait bounds (*bounded parametric polymorphism*), or **trait objects**, the next lesson.

points: Structs and enums with methods are objects in all but name.
Privacy gives encapsulation: hide fields, expose methods, change the inside freely.
No inheritance: use default trait methods for shared behavior and composition for shared data.
Polymorphism comes from generics, trait objects and enums.
